title: Design High-Performing Architectures
intro: Domain 3 is the 'pick the right service and prove you know its numbers' domain — about 16 of 65 questions. It almost never asks 'is this secure' or 'is this cheap'; it asks which service class matches the access pattern, and then whether you know the one limit that rules out the tempting alternative. Three mental models unlock nearly all of it. First, storage sorts into block (one instance, raw device), file (many instances, POSIX or SMB path), and object (HTTP, infinite scale) — the question tells you the protocol and the protocol picks the service. Second, performance problems are solved by moving work closer (cache, edge, read replica) or by widening the pipe (more shards, more prefixes, bigger network), never by 'upgrading the instance' unless the stem says CPU-bound. Third, every managed service has a shard-shaped unit — an EBS IOPS ceiling, a Kinesis shard, a DynamoDB partition, a VPN tunnel — and the exam tests whether you can spot that the workload exceeds one unit. Learn the numbers; the discriminating fact is usually numeric.

sections.title: Storage picker: block, file, object
sections.summary: The access protocol in the scenario (raw device / POSIX / SMB / HTTP) determines the storage family, and the throughput or IOPS figure determines the tier inside it.

concepts.name: Block vs file vs object, and choosing an EBS volume type
concepts.explain:
Block storage is a raw device attached to one instance at a time — the OS puts a filesystem on it. File storage speaks a network filesystem protocol (NFS or SMB) so many instances mount the same tree at once. Object storage is an HTTP API with no partial writes, no filesystem semantics, and effectively unlimited capacity. A scenario that says 'the application writes to a local path and cannot be modified' with one server is block; the same sentence with 'fleet of instances share the files' is file; 'store user uploads and serve them to the internet' is object.
Inside EBS, gp3 is the modern default because performance is decoupled from size: every gp3 volume gets 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s baseline regardless of whether it is 1 GiB or 16 TiB, and you provision up to 16,000 IOPS and 1,000 MB/s independently. gp2 tied performance to size at 3 IOPS per GiB, which is why the classic exam story is 'we had to over-provision a 4 TiB gp2 volume just to get IOPS' — the answer is migrate to gp3, cheaper and faster. io1/io2 exist only when you need more than 16,000 IOPS or sub-millisecond consistency; io2 Block Express reaches 256,000 IOPS and 4,000 MB/s, and io1 and io2 are the only types that support Multi-Attach for clustered filesystems. st1 and sc1 are spinning disks sold by throughput, not IOPS — big sequential scans (log processing, data warehouse staging, MapReduce) — and they cannot be boot volumes.
concepts.exam_tests: Trigger words map almost one-to-one. 'Over-provisioned for IOPS' or 'need more IOPS without more capacity' means gp3. 'More than 16,000 IOPS' or 'sub-millisecond latency, mission-critical database' means io2 Block Express. 'Shared block device for a clustered application like a Linux cluster manager' means io2 Multi-Attach, not EFS. 'Large sequential streaming workloads, big data, log processing, lowest cost per TB' means st1; 'infrequently accessed, cold, lowest cost' means sc1. 'Highest possible IOPS, data is temporary or replicated by the application' means instance store, not any EBS type.

example.scenario: A company runs a self-managed PostgreSQL server on a 500 GiB gp2 volume. Monitoring shows the volume is throttled at 1,500 IOPS while only 40 percent of capacity is used. The team needs at least 8,000 IOPS and wants the lowest cost.
example.answer: Change the volume type to gp3 and provision 8,000 IOPS at the existing 500 GiB size.
example.why: gp2 gives 3 IOPS per GiB, so 500 GiB caps at 1,500 IOPS and the only gp2 fix is to grow the volume to ~2.7 TiB of storage you do not need. gp3 decouples the two, so you buy 8,000 IOPS on a 500 GiB volume. io1 would also work but costs materially more per provisioned IOPS, and the stem asks for lowest cost.

3 IOPS per GiB, burst to 3,000 under 1 TiB
Legacy only — the exam wants you to migrate off it
Provisioned IOPS, max 50:1 IOPS per GiB
High IOPS on older instance families
Tier-1 databases, sub-ms latency, Multi-Attach clusters
Sequential big-data, log processing, ETL staging
Rarely accessed bulk data, lowest EBS cost per GB

gotchas: HDD volumes (st1, sc1) cannot be used as boot volumes — an option offering sc1 for a root volume is always wrong.
Instance store data is lost on stop, hibernate, or terminate; it survives only a reboot. 'Must persist' kills it instantly.
EBS Multi-Attach is io1/io2 only, same Availability Zone only, up to 16 instances, and needs a cluster-aware filesystem — it is not a substitute for EFS.
EBS volumes are AZ-scoped; to move one to another AZ you snapshot and restore, which the exam phrases as 'copy the snapshot'.
gp3 throughput is capped at 0.25 MB/s per provisioned IOPS, so you cannot buy 1,000 MB/s on a 3,000 IOPS volume.
Changing volume type or size is an online operation (Elastic Volumes) — answers claiming downtime is required are wrong.

gp2: 3 IOPS per GiB, 16,000 IOPS ceiling
io2 Block Express: 256,000 IOPS, 4,000 MB/s, up to 64 TiB
st1 max 500 MB/s, sc1 max 250 MB/s
Multi-Attach: up to 16 instances, same AZ, io1/io2 only
concepts.mnemonic: gp3 = 3,000 free IOPS. io2 = I/O to the max. st1 = STreaming. sc1 = SCarcely used.

concepts.name: Shared file systems: EFS vs the four FSx flavours
concepts.explain:
The moment a scenario needs many instances writing to the same directory tree, you are in file-storage land and the only question is which protocol and which OS. EFS is NFS for Linux: elastic, pay per GB stored, no capacity to provision, and it is Regional by default (data replicated across AZs) with a cheaper One Zone option. FSx for Windows File Server is SMB with NTFS ACLs and Active Directory integration — the tell is 'Windows', 'SMB share', 'AD-joined', or 'DFS namespaces'. FSx for Lustre is the HPC and machine-learning parallel filesystem: hundreds of GB/s, sub-millisecond latency, and a native S3 link so a Lustre filesystem can be a fast POSIX front end over an S3 bucket. FSx for NetApp ONTAP is the multi-protocol answer — NFS, SMB and iSCSI at once, plus ONTAP features (snapshots, cloning, dedup, SnapMirror) that on-prem NetApp customers want to keep. FSx for OpenZFS is the ZFS/Linux-NFS lift-and-shift with very high IOPS and snapshots.
EFS has two dimensions people confuse. Performance mode is General Purpose (lowest latency, the default and correct answer almost always) versus Max I/O (higher aggregate throughput, higher per-operation latency, now legacy). Throughput mode is Bursting (scales with stored data, uses credits), Elastic (scales automatically, pay per GB transferred, the modern default for spiky workloads) or Provisioned (fixed throughput when you need more than storage size gives you).
concepts.exam_tests: 'Windows application, SMB, Active Directory' is FSx for Windows every time — EFS is never the answer for Windows. 'HPC cluster', 'machine learning training', 'sub-millisecond, hundreds of GB/s', or 'process data that lives in S3 with a POSIX interface' is FSx for Lustre. 'Migrate a NetApp appliance' or 'needs NFS and SMB access to the same data' is ONTAP. 'Linux fleet, shared, grows automatically, no capacity planning' is EFS. If only one instance touches the data, the answer is EBS and the file-system options are all distractors.

example.scenario: A genomics company runs a 500-node HPC cluster that must read a 40 TB reference dataset already stored in Amazon S3 and write results back. The jobs are throughput-bound and need a POSIX filesystem. The cluster runs for six hours a day and is then torn down.
example.answer: Create an FSx for Lustre scratch filesystem linked to the S3 bucket, and export results back to S3.
example.why: Lustre is the only AWS filesystem that both hits HPC throughput and links natively to S3, lazily loading objects on first read and exporting changes back. Scratch is correct because the cluster is transient and the durable copy lives in S3, so paying for persistent replication adds cost with no benefit. EFS would work functionally but cannot reach the aggregate throughput and has no S3 linkage.

rows: Shared Linux app data, CMS, home directories, Lambda/ECS shared state
AD-joined Windows shares, DFS namespaces, .NET apps
HPC, ML training, S3-linked high-throughput processing
NetApp migration, multi-protocol, snapshots and dedup
ZFS or Linux NFS server lift-and-shift, very high IOPS

gotchas: EFS One Zone is cheaper but loses the AZ-failure resilience — never pick it when the stem says highly available.
FSx for Lustre scratch filesystems have no replication; a failed host loses data. Persistent is the answer whenever the data is not reproducible from S3.

EFS Infrequent Access and Archive classes need a lifecycle policy to be useful, and on Bursting or Provisioned throughput modes reads from IA carry a per-GB retrieval charge — that charge can make a hot dataset in IA more expensive than Standard.
EFS Access Points enforce a POSIX user and root directory per application — the standard answer for multi-tenant directory isolation on one filesystem.
Max I/O performance mode raises per-operation latency; if the stem says 'lowest latency', it is General Purpose (or Elastic throughput), not Max I/O.
FSx for Windows supports DFS Namespaces to present multiple filesystems as one namespace, and that is how you scale past a single filesystem's limits.

FSx for Lustre: sub-millisecond latency, hundreds of GB/s aggregate throughput
EBS Multi-Attach: 16 instances, same AZ, io1/io2 only

concepts.name: S3 performance: prefixes, multipart, byte-range, acceleration
concepts.explain:
S3 scales request rate per prefix, not per bucket. Each prefix sustains 3,500 PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE and 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second, and there is no limit on the number of prefixes — so the fix for a request-rate ceiling is always to spread keys across more prefixes, never to create more buckets. This is why the classic date-based key of year/month/day/ hurts: every write on a given day lands in one prefix. Randomising or hashing the leading characters spreads load.
For large objects, multipart upload is the performance answer: parallel part uploads, retry of a single failed part instead of the whole object, and required above 5 GB. AWS recommends it above 100 MB. The read-side mirror is byte-range fetches — request parts of an object in parallel, or fetch just the header of a large file instead of the whole thing. Transfer Acceleration solves a different problem: clients far from the bucket Region upload over the CloudFront edge network and then across the AWS backbone, which helps only when distance and public-internet latency are the bottleneck. S3 Express One Zone is the low-latency tier: directory buckets in a single AZ, an order of magnitude faster first-byte latency, much cheaper requests, but higher storage price and no AZ redundancy.
concepts.exam_tests: '503 Slow Down errors' or 'request rate exceeded' means add prefixes. 'Uploading 5 GB files over an unreliable network' or 'improve upload throughput and resume failed parts' means multipart. 'Global users uploading to a single bucket, high latency' means Transfer Acceleration (or CloudFront for downloads). 'Only needs the first few KB of each large object' means byte-range fetch. 'Millisecond-scale, request-heavy analytics on hot data in one AZ' means S3 Express One Zone.

example.scenario: A media company writes 20,000 small objects per second into one S3 bucket using keys of the form logs/2026-09-05/<uuid>. The application receives frequent HTTP 503 Slow Down responses. Cost and code changes should be minimal.
example.answer: Change the key naming so writes are spread across many prefixes, for example logs/<hash>/2026-09-05/<uuid>.
example.why: The 3,500 write-requests-per-second limit is per prefix, and every object that day shares one prefix. Spreading across 8 or 16 hash prefixes multiplies the ceiling linearly. Creating additional buckets is unnecessary operational overhead, and Transfer Acceleration addresses network distance, not request-rate throttling.

rows: Exceeds 3,500 PUT or 5,500 GET per second
Objects over 100 MB; mandatory over 5 GB
Only need part of a large object

gotchas: S3 request limits are per prefix, not per bucket — 'create multiple buckets' is a distractor.
Maximum single object is 5 TB; maximum single PUT without multipart is 5 GB.
Transfer Acceleration costs extra per GB and must be enabled on the bucket; it does nothing for clients in the same Region.
S3 Express One Zone stores data in one AZ and uses directory buckets — it is not a durability upgrade and cannot replace S3 Standard for critical data.
S3 is strongly read-after-write consistent for all operations now — any answer that says 'wait for eventual consistency' is stale and wrong.
CloudFront in front of S3 reduces both latency and S3 request cost, which is why it appears as the answer to 'reduce load on the origin'.
numbers: 3,500 write / 5,500 read requests per second per prefix
Multipart recommended above 100 MB, required above 5 GB
Multipart: up to 10,000 parts, each 5 MB to 5 GB (last part may be smaller)
Max object size 5 TB

sections.title: Compute picker: instances, placement, scaling, serverless
sections.summary: Match the instance family letter to the bottleneck, the placement group to the failure or latency requirement, and the scaling policy to how predictable demand is.

concepts.name: EC2 instance families, Graviton, and the network stack (ENA vs EFA)
concepts.explain:
Instance types encode their purpose in the first letter. C is compute (high CPU-to-memory), M is the balanced middle, R is memory-optimised, X and u- are extreme memory, I is local NVMe storage, D is dense HDD, P is GPU for training, G is GPU for inference and graphics, and T is burstable for spiky low-average workloads. T instances earn CPU credits when idle and spend them under load; in standard mode they throttle when credits run out, and in unlimited mode they keep running and you pay a surcharge. A trailing g means Graviton, AWS's ARM processor, which typically delivers materially better price-performance but requires ARM-compatible binaries or containers.
Networking has two levels. The Elastic Network Adapter is standard enhanced networking, reaching 100 Gbps and beyond on the largest current instances, and ENA Express uses the SRD protocol to lift single-flow throughput. The Elastic Fabric Adapter is a different animal: it bypasses the operating system kernel so MPI and NCCL libraries talk directly to the hardware, which is what HPC and distributed ML training need. EFA is the answer whenever you see 'tightly coupled', 'MPI', 'NCCL', or 'inter-node communication is the bottleneck'.
concepts.exam_tests: The stem names the bottleneck and you name the letter. 'In-memory database, SAP HANA, large caches' is R or X. 'Batch encoding, gaming servers, high-performance web' is C. 'Millions of local IOPS, NoSQL, data warehouse scratch' is I. 'Low average CPU with occasional spikes, cost-sensitive' is T with unlimited mode. 'Tightly coupled HPC' is EFA plus a cluster placement group. 'Reduce compute cost with no architecture change on a Linux container workload' is Graviton.

example.scenario: A research team runs a weather simulation across 60 EC2 instances using MPI. Profiling shows the job spends most of its wall time in inter-node message passing, and the team wants the lowest possible latency between nodes.
example.answer: Launch the fleet in a cluster placement group using instances with an Elastic Fabric Adapter.
example.why: EFA bypasses the kernel network stack for MPI traffic, which is the specific bottleneck named, and a cluster placement group puts the nodes on the same low-latency network segment. Adding more or bigger instances does not help a communication-bound job, and a spread placement group deliberately separates instances, which is the opposite of what is needed.

columns: Pick it when the stem says
rows: Small workloads, dev/test, spiky traffic, cheapest baseline
No stated bottleneck; typical application servers
CPU-bound, batch, media encoding, HPC front end, ad serving
In-memory cache, large database, SAP HANA, big joins
Highest local IOPS, NoSQL, data warehouse, dense HDD

gotchas: T instances in standard mode throttle to baseline once credits are exhausted — the fix for 'performance degrades after some time' is unlimited mode or a move to M.
Graviton requires recompiled or multi-arch container images; an option that says 'switch to Graviton with no code changes' on a Windows or x86-only binary workload is wrong.
EFA only accelerates traffic between instances in the same subnet and works best inside a cluster placement group; it does not speed up traffic leaving the VPC.
Enhanced networking (ENA) is on by default on current generations — 'enable enhanced networking' as a fix is usually a distractor on modern instance types.
Instance network bandwidth is shared with EBS unless the instance is EBS-optimised, which is default on current families.
Nitro-based instances are required for the highest EBS performance figures such as io2 Block Express.
concepts.mnemonic: C = CPU, R = RAM, I = IOPS, D = Dense disk, G/P = GPU, T = Tiny/bursty, M = Middle.

concepts.name: Placement groups: cluster, spread, partition
concepts.explain: Placement groups tell EC2 how to physically position instances relative to each other, and each one solves a different problem. A cluster placement group packs instances into a single rack in one AZ so they get the lowest network latency and highest single-flow bandwidth between them — the trade-off is correlated failure, since one rack event affects everything. A spread placement group does the opposite: every instance goes on distinct underlying hardware with its own power and network, which is why it is capped at seven running instances per AZ per group. It is for a small number of critical, independent instances such as domain controllers or a quorum. A partition placement group is the middle ground built for distributed data stores: up to seven partitions per AZ, each on its own set of racks, and instances learn their partition through metadata so software like HDFS, HBase, Cassandra and Kafka can place replicas in different partitions.
concepts.exam_tests: 'Lowest latency between nodes' or 'tightly coupled HPC' is cluster. 'Small number of critical instances that must not share hardware' is spread, and if the count exceeds seven per AZ the option is impossible. 'Large distributed data store, replicas must not share a rack, hundreds of instances' is partition. The seven-per-AZ number on spread is a favourite discriminator.

example.scenario: A company deploys a 30-node Cassandra ring across three Availability Zones and wants replica nodes to survive a rack-level hardware failure without losing more than one replica.
example.answer: Use a partition placement group with partitions spread across the three Availability Zones.
example.why: Partition groups isolate racks and expose partition identity so Cassandra can place replicas in different partitions, which is exactly the rack-fault-isolation requirement. A spread group cannot hold 30 instances since it allows only seven running instances per AZ, and a cluster group concentrates the risk instead of spreading it.

rows: Bounded by capacity of one AZ/rack
HPC, MPI, low-latency and high-throughput node-to-node
Distinct hardware, separate power and network
7 running instances per AZ per group
Small set of critical instances that must fail independently
Groups of racks, isolated per partition
7 partitions per AZ, many instances each
HDFS, HBase, Cassandra, Kafka — replica placement

gotchas: Spread groups allow only seven running instances per Availability Zone — any option asking for more in one spread group is invalid.
Cluster placement groups live in a single AZ, so they trade availability for latency; they are never the answer to a high-availability stem.
You cannot merge placement groups, and moving a running instance into one requires it to be stopped.
Cluster groups work best when all instances are launched at once with the same instance type; a later launch can fail with insufficient capacity.
You cannot launch instances onto a Dedicated Host inside a placement group — the two features are mutually exclusive.
A placement group is free — cost is never a reason to reject one.
numbers: Spread: 7 running instances per AZ per group
Partition: up to 7 partitions per AZ
concepts.mnemonic: Cluster = Close. Spread = Separate (7 per AZ). Partition = Per-rack groups for big data.

concepts.name: Auto Scaling policies: target tracking, step, scheduled, predictive
concepts.explain:
Auto Scaling questions come down to how much you know about future demand. If you know nothing but you have a metric that represents load, use target tracking: pick a metric such as average CPU or ALBRequestCountPerTarget and a target value, and Auto Scaling creates the alarms and does the math. It is the default correct answer and the one with the least operational overhead. Step scaling is for when the response should differ by how badly the threshold is breached — add two instances at 60 percent, add six at 90 percent. Simple scaling is its legacy predecessor and should never be the answer. Scheduled scaling is for calendar-known patterns: business hours, a batch window, a Monday morning spike. Predictive scaling uses machine learning over at least 24 hours (ideally 14 days) of history to forecast the next 48 hours and provisions capacity in advance, which is the answer when the stem complains that reactive scaling is too slow for a recurring daily pattern.
Two supporting mechanisms matter. Cooldown (default 300 seconds) stops a policy from firing again while the previous action settles. Warm pools keep pre-initialised instances in a stopped or hibernated state so a long boot or application-warm-up does not delay scale-out, which is the answer whenever the stem says instances take many minutes to become useful.
concepts.exam_tests: 'Least operational overhead' plus a maintainable metric equals target tracking. 'Traffic increases every weekday at 9am' equals scheduled. 'Cyclical, recurring pattern, and reactive scaling lags behind' equals predictive. 'Application takes 15 minutes to warm up and users see errors during scale-out' equals a warm pool (or lifecycle hooks). 'Different responses depending on how far the metric is over the threshold' equals step scaling.

example.scenario: A retail application sees a large, repeatable traffic spike every day between 18:00 and 21:00. Instances take about eight minutes to boot and register, and users report slow responses during the first 20 minutes of the spike even though CPU-based scaling is configured.
example.answer: Add predictive scaling (or scheduled scaling) so capacity is provisioned before the spike, keeping target tracking for unexpected load.
example.why: Reactive target tracking only acts after the metric moves, and an eight-minute boot means capacity always arrives late. Predictive scaling forecasts the recurring daily pattern and warms capacity ahead of it; scheduled scaling achieves the same when the pattern is fixed and known. Lowering the CPU target only wastes capacity all day without removing the lag.

rows: A single metric against a target value
Default choice; keep CPU at 50 percent or requests per target at N
One alarm, one adjustment, then cooldown
Never — superseded by target tracking and step
Recurring cyclical demand where boot time causes lag
Long boot or application warm-up times

gotchas: Predictive scaling needs at least 24 hours of history and only adds capacity; you still need target tracking to scale in and to handle surprises.
Default cooldown is 300 seconds; too long a cooldown is a classic cause of 'the group scales too slowly'.
Health check grace period must exceed application start-up time, or the ASG kills instances before they pass the load balancer health check.
Attaching an ALB and using ELB health checks (rather than EC2 status checks) is what makes the ASG replace instances whose application has failed but whose OS is fine.
Auto Scaling never scales the instance size — an option that says 'scale vertically automatically' is wrong for ASG.
Lifecycle hooks pause instances in Pending:Wait or Terminating:Wait so you can bootstrap or drain; they are the answer for 'run a script before an instance goes into service'.

Predictive scaling forecasts up to 48 hours ahead from at least 24 hours of history

concepts.name: Lambda limits, and the serverless-versus-container decision
concepts.explain:
Lambda's limits are the most frequently tested numbers in this domain because they are the discriminating fact that eliminates it as an answer. Fifteen minutes maximum execution, 128 MB to 10,240 MB of memory (CPU scales with memory, so raising memory is how you make a Lambda faster), 10 GB of ephemeral /tmp, a 6 MB synchronous request and response payload, and 256 KB for asynchronous events and for SQS or SNS messages. Cold starts are addressed by provisioned concurrency (keeps initialised environments warm, costs per hour) or SnapStart (caches a snapshot of the initialised runtime for Java, Python and .NET; no extra charge on Java managed runtimes, while Python and .NET bill for snapshot cache and restore).
When the limits do not fit, you move up the container ladder. ECS on Fargate removes host management and bills per task — the low-overhead default for containers. ECS on EC2 gives you GPUs, Spot control, larger local storage and better economics at sustained high utilisation. EKS is the answer when the stem says Kubernetes, portability, or an existing Kubernetes toolchain. App Runner is the simplest path from a container image or repository to an HTTPS service. AWS Batch handles queued batch jobs with dependencies and Spot. Elastic Beanstalk is the 'deploy my app without learning the infrastructure but keep the EC2 instances visible' option.
concepts.exam_tests: Any workload described as running longer than 15 minutes rules Lambda out and points at Fargate, Batch or EC2. 'Large payload' beyond 6 MB means write to S3 and pass a reference. 'Cold start latency for a Java API' means SnapStart or provisioned concurrency. 'Needs a shared filesystem across invocations' means mount EFS to Lambda. 'Existing Kubernetes manifests' means EKS. 'Long-running batch jobs with dependencies and Spot' means AWS Batch.

example.scenario: A team processes uploaded video files with a job that takes 25 to 40 minutes and needs 8 vCPUs and 30 GB of memory. Uploads arrive irregularly, a few dozen per day, and the team does not want to manage servers.
example.answer: Run the job as an ECS task on Fargate, triggered by the upload event (AWS Batch on Fargate is equally valid).
example.why: The 15-minute Lambda timeout and 10 GB memory ceiling both eliminate Lambda regardless of how the code is written. Fargate has no execution time limit, supports the required vCPU and memory, and still removes server management. Provisioning an EC2 Auto Scaling group would work but adds host management the stem explicitly rejects.

rows: Any long-running batch or transcoding job
Large in-memory processing; note CPU scales with memory
Working with very large files locally
Large uploads through API Gateway — use S3 presigned URLs
Large SNS/SQS/EventBridge messages — use the claim-check pattern
50 MB zipped, 250 MB unzipped, 10 GB container image
Fat dependency trees — use layers or a container image
Very high fan-out without a quota increase

gotchas: Increasing Lambda memory increases CPU proportionally — the standard answer to 'the function is too slow' when the code cannot change.
Provisioned concurrency costs money whether used or not; SnapStart works only on Java, Python and .NET managed runtimes, and is free of extra charge only on Java.
Reserved concurrency both guarantees and caps a function's concurrency — it is how you protect a downstream database from a Lambda storm.
Lambda inside a VPC uses Hyperplane ENIs and no longer has the old cold-start penalty, but it still needs a NAT gateway or VPC endpoints for AWS API calls.
Fargate does not support GPUs, privileged containers, or host networking — those requirements force the EC2 launch type.
Elastic Beanstalk is not serverless; it provisions EC2 instances you can see and pay for.

6 MB synchronous payload, 256 KB asynchronous payload
