sections.title: Database picker: relational, key-value, cache, purpose-built
sections.summary: Data shape and access pattern choose the engine; read scaling, connection handling and caching choose the fix when the engine is right but slow.

concepts.name: Relational scaling: RDS, Aurora, read replicas and RDS Proxy
concepts.explain:
For relational workloads the exam splits three ways: read scaling, write scaling, and connection scaling. Read scaling is read replicas — up to fifteen for RDS for MySQL, MariaDB and PostgreSQL (five for Oracle and SQL Server), and up to fifteen Aurora replicas behind a reader endpoint. Read replicas are asynchronous and exist for performance, not for high availability; Multi-AZ is the availability answer, and confusing the two is the single most common trap in this area. Write scaling on relational is hard: you go bigger, or you shard, or you move the hot part to DynamoDB.
Aurora's architecture is what gets tested. Storage is a shared distributed volume that auto-grows in 10 GB increments up to 128 TiB and keeps six copies across three AZs, which is why adding a replica is fast and cheap — replicas attach to the same storage instead of copying data. The cluster endpoint always points at the writer, the reader endpoint load-balances across replicas, and custom endpoints let you route, say, reporting queries to specific larger instances. Parallel query pushes work down into the storage layer for analytical scans. Aurora Serverless v2 scales in Aurora Capacity Units where one ACU is roughly 2 GiB of memory, adjusting in 0.5-ACU steps within seconds, and on recent engine versions the minimum can be set to 0 ACUs so an idle cluster scales to zero.
RDS Proxy solves the connection problem. Thousands of concurrent Lambda invocations each opening a database connection exhausts the engine's connection limit; RDS Proxy pools and multiplexes those connections, and it also shortens failover time because clients hold their connection to the proxy.
concepts.exam_tests: 'Too many connections' or 'Lambda spikes overwhelm the database' is RDS Proxy. 'Reporting queries slow down the production workload' is a read replica plus the reader or a custom endpoint. 'Unpredictable and intermittent load, do not want to size an instance' is Aurora Serverless v2. 'Needs to survive an AZ failure automatically' is Multi-AZ, not a read replica. 'Sub-second cross-Region reads and disaster recovery' is Aurora Global Database.

example.scenario: A serverless API backed by Lambda writes to an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL instance. During traffic spikes the functions fail with too-many-connections errors, although CPU on the database stays below 30 percent.
example.answer: Put RDS Proxy in front of the database and have Lambda connect through the proxy.
example.why: The failure is connection exhaustion, not compute — CPU at 30 percent proves the instance is not the bottleneck, so scaling it up buys connections only incidentally and expensively. RDS Proxy pools and reuses connections so thousands of invocations share a small pool. Read replicas do not help because the workload is writes.

rows: Read replicas are async and need manual promotion
Multi-AZ standby serves no reads (single-instance Multi-AZ)
Aurora custom endpoint or a dedicated replica
Bigger writer instance costs more and still contends
Scaling instance size raises connections only marginally
Provisioned instances need a peak-sized guess
Cross-Region read replica has higher lag and slower failover
Analytical scans over the OLTP data
Aurora parallel query or Redshift zero-ETL
Running them on the writer starves transactions

gotchas: Read replicas are for performance; Multi-AZ is for availability. The exam swaps these deliberately.
The single-instance RDS Multi-AZ standby is not readable; the Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment gives two readable standbys and faster failover.
Aurora storage grows automatically to 128 TiB — 'provision more storage' is never the Aurora answer.
Aurora replicas double as failover targets with a priority tier, so they give both read scaling and HA; plain RDS read replicas do not fail over automatically.
RDS Proxy must live in the VPC and is not internet-accessible; it also enforces IAM authentication and Secrets Manager credentials.
Aurora Serverless v2 scales in place without dropping connections; v1 paused and had cold starts — do not carry v1 behaviour into a v2 answer.
numbers: RDS read replicas: up to 15 for MySQL, MariaDB and PostgreSQL (5 for Oracle and SQL Server); Aurora: up to 15 replicas
Aurora storage: 10 GB increments to 128 TiB, six copies across three AZs
Aurora Serverless v2: 1 ACU is roughly 2 GiB of memory, 0.5-ACU scaling steps, minimum 0 ACUs on supported versions

concepts.name: DynamoDB: partition keys, indexes, capacity and DAX
concepts.explain:
DynamoDB performance is a partition-key design problem. The table is split into partitions, and each physical partition sustains about 3,000 read capacity units, 1,000 write capacity units and 10 GB. If your partition key has low cardinality or a skewed distribution — a status field, a single tenant ID, today's date — all traffic lands on one partition and you get throttling while the table-level capacity looks fine. That is the hot partition problem, and the fix is a higher-cardinality key or write sharding by appending a suffix. Adaptive capacity now isolates hot partitions automatically and borrows unused throughput, but it cannot rescue a key with only three possible values.
Indexes come in two flavours. A global secondary index has its own partition and sort key and its own provisioned capacity, is eventually consistent only, and can be added at any time. A local secondary index shares the table's partition key, offers a different sort key, supports strongly consistent reads, shares table capacity, and must be created with the table. If a scenario needs a completely different access pattern, it is a GSI; if it needs another sort order on the same item collection, it can be an LSI.
Capacity mode is a cost and predictability decision: on-demand for unknown or spiky traffic with no capacity planning, provisioned with auto scaling for steady predictable traffic at lower cost. DAX is the read accelerator — a DynamoDB-specific, in-VPC write-through cache that turns single-digit-millisecond reads into microseconds without any application rewrite.
concepts.exam_tests: 'Throttling on a small number of items despite plenty of provisioned capacity' is a hot partition. 'Microsecond read latency for DynamoDB with minimal code change' is DAX, never ElastiCache. 'Query by a different attribute' is a GSI. 'Automatically delete records after N days' is TTL. 'React to every item change' is DynamoDB Streams into Lambda. 'Unpredictable traffic, no capacity planning' is on-demand mode.

example.scenario: An IoT platform stores telemetry in DynamoDB with the partition key set to the device model (about 12 values) and a sort key of timestamp. Writes are throttled during peak hours even though only 40 percent of provisioned WCUs are consumed at the table level.
example.answer: Redesign the partition key to the device ID (or device ID plus a shard suffix) so writes spread across many partitions.
example.why: Twelve distinct partition-key values means writes concentrate on twelve partitions, each capped at 1,000 WCU, so the table appears under-utilised while individual partitions throttle. Raising table capacity spreads across more partitions but keeps the same skew and wastes money. DAX would not help because the problem is writes, and DAX accelerates reads.

gotchas: One RCU is one strongly consistent read of up to 4 KB per second, or two eventually consistent reads; one WCU is one write of up to 1 KB per second.
Maximum item size is 400 KB — larger payloads go to S3 with a pointer stored in the item.
DAX caches reads only, and strongly consistent reads bypass the cache entirely.
TTL deletions are best-effort and can take up to 48 hours to appear — never the answer when the stem requires immediate deletion.
Switching between on-demand and provisioned can be done only once every 24 hours per table.
Scans are the wrong answer nearly always; if an option says 'Scan with a filter', look for the Query or GSI option instead.
numbers: Per partition: ~3,000 RCU, ~1,000 WCU, 10 GB
Item size limit 400 KB
Streams retention 24 hours (365 days via Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB)
concepts.mnemonic: GSI = Global = anything goes, own capacity. LSI = Local = Locked to the table's key and created at Launch.

concepts.name: Caching: ElastiCache Redis vs Memcached vs DAX vs MemoryDB
concepts.explain:
Caching questions test two things: which cache engine, and which caching strategy. Memcached is a simple multi-threaded key-value cache with no persistence, no replication and no failover — you scale it by adding nodes and the client shards across them. Redis (now ElastiCache for Valkey or Redis OSS) has data structures (sorted sets, lists, hashes), replication with automatic failover, Multi-AZ, backups, pub/sub and transactions, which makes it the answer for leaderboards, session stores that must survive a node failure, and anything needing more than plain strings. MemoryDB is the durable version: a Redis-compatible primary database with a multi-AZ transactional log, microsecond reads and single-digit-millisecond writes, used when the in-memory store is the system of record rather than a cache. DAX is neither — it is a DynamoDB-only, API-compatible cache that requires no application changes.
Strategies matter too. Lazy loading (cache-aside) only populates on a miss, so the cache holds just what is asked for, but the first request after a miss pays the full latency and data can go stale. Write-through updates the cache on every write, so reads are always fresh, but you pay a write penalty and cache data nobody reads. Adding a TTL to either bounds staleness, and the combination of lazy loading plus TTL is the standard pragmatic answer.
concepts.exam_tests: 'Session store that must survive a node failure' or 'leaderboard' or 'needs replication and Multi-AZ' is Redis. 'Simple object caching, multi-threaded, scale horizontally, no persistence needed' is Memcached. 'DynamoDB reads in microseconds with no application rewrite' is DAX. 'In-memory with durability, as the primary database' is MemoryDB. 'Stale data appears after an update' points at write-through or a shorter TTL.

example.scenario: An e-commerce site stores shopping-cart sessions in an ElastiCache for Memcached cluster. When a node fails, affected customers lose their carts. The company wants the same in-memory latency without losing sessions on a node failure and with minimal application redesign.
example.answer: Move the session store to ElastiCache for Redis with replication and Multi-AZ automatic failover enabled.
example.why: Memcached has no replication or persistence, so a lost node is lost data by design — no configuration fixes it. Redis replicates to a replica in another AZ and fails over automatically, keeping the same key-value latency profile. DynamoDB would also survive the failure but is a larger redesign than the stem allows, and DAX is irrelevant since there is no DynamoDB table.

rows: Simple caching, multi-threaded, horizontal node scaling
Snapshots (backups), not a system of record
Durable — writes committed to the log before acknowledgement
In-memory as the primary database of record
Microsecond DynamoDB reads, no code change
Static and cacheable dynamic content near users

gotchas: Memcached cannot do Multi-AZ failover or backups — any stem mentioning durability, replication or persistence eliminates it.
DAX only fronts DynamoDB; using ElastiCache for a DynamoDB cache is possible but requires application changes, which loses on 'minimal changes'.
Redis cluster mode enabled shards the keyspace and is how you scale writes and memory past one node; cluster mode disabled scales reads only.
Lazy loading serves stale data until eviction or TTL; write-through guarantees freshness but caches items that may never be read.
Caching in front of a database only helps read-heavy workloads — an option offering a cache for a write-heavy problem is a distractor.
ElastiCache is in-VPC and not internet-accessible; it also does not encrypt in transit unless you enable it.
concepts.mnemonic: Memcached = Mere cache. Redis = Rich and Resilient. MemoryDB = Memory that is a Database. DAX = DynamoDB Accelerator, nothing else.

concepts.name: Purpose-built databases and migrating into them
concepts.explain:
The exam gives you a data shape and expects the matching engine. Highly connected data with relationship traversal (fraud rings, social graphs, recommendations) is Neptune. JSON documents with a MongoDB API is DocumentDB. Wide-column Cassandra workloads are Keyspaces. Time-stamped measurements at massive scale with time-window queries are Timestream. Full-text search, log analytics and observability dashboards are OpenSearch Service. Petabyte-scale analytical SQL over structured data with complex joins and aggregations is Redshift — a columnar MPP warehouse where RA3 nodes separate compute from managed storage, Spectrum extends queries to data still sitting in S3, and Redshift Serverless removes cluster sizing entirely.
Getting data in is a two-tool story. Database Migration Service moves the data and can run continuous change data capture so the source stays live until cutover. It requires the target to already exist and works both homogeneously (Oracle to Oracle) and heterogeneously (Oracle to Aurora PostgreSQL). For heterogeneous moves you first run the Schema Conversion Tool to translate schema, stored procedures and application SQL. The rule to memorise: SCT converts the schema, DMS moves the rows.
concepts.exam_tests: 'Relationships between entities, traverse connections' is Neptune. 'MongoDB workload with minimal application change' is DocumentDB. 'Cassandra, CQL, serverless' is Keyspaces. 'Trillions of events per day with time-based queries and automatic tiering' is Timestream. 'Search across documents, log analytics, Kibana-style dashboards' is OpenSearch. 'Complex analytical queries joining terabytes' is Redshift; if the data is already in S3 and should stay there, Spectrum or Athena. 'Migrate with minimal downtime' is DMS with CDC.

example.scenario: A bank stores 15 years of transaction history in Amazon S3 in Parquet format and wants analysts to run complex joins between that history and the current-quarter data held in a Redshift cluster, without duplicating the historical data.
example.answer: Use Redshift Spectrum to query the S3 data as external tables and join it to the cluster's local tables.
example.why: Spectrum exists precisely to join warehouse tables with data that stays in S3, using the Glue Data Catalog for schema. Loading 15 years into the cluster duplicates storage and defeats the requirement. Athena can query the S3 data but cannot join it to tables that live inside the Redshift cluster.

rows: Lift-and-shift a commercial or open-source database
Instance or ACUs, shared 128 TiB storage
IoT and telemetry with time-window queries

gotchas: Redshift is a warehouse, not an OLTP database — an option using it for high-concurrency single-row transactions is wrong.
OpenSearch is not a database of record; it indexes data that lives elsewhere.
DMS requires the target schema to exist; for heterogeneous migrations run the Schema Conversion Tool first.
DMS continuous replication (CDC) is what enables minimal-downtime cutovers — plain full load implies an outage window.
Amazon QLDB is retired; ledger-style immutability questions in older banks now resolve to Aurora PostgreSQL with verifiable history or to purpose-built application design.
Timestream automatically tiers from a memory store to a magnetic store by retention policy, which is why it beats building the same thing on DynamoDB.

sections.title: Network performance: edge, hybrid links, and VPC interconnects
sections.summary: Latency for end users is solved at the edge, latency and bandwidth for on-premises is solved by the link type, and connectivity between many VPCs is solved by picking the right interconnect topology.

concepts.name: CloudFront vs Global Accelerator (and Route 53 latency routing)
concepts.explain:
All three reduce user-perceived latency, but by different mechanisms, and the exam separates them cleanly. CloudFront is a content delivery network: it caches HTTP and HTTPS responses at hundreds of edge locations, so the second and subsequent users get a response without ever reaching the origin. Cache behaviour is controlled by cache policies (which headers, cookies and query strings form the cache key) and origin request policies. Origin groups give automatic failover to a secondary origin on defined 4xx or 5xx responses, and Origin Shield adds a regional caching tier that raises the cache-hit ratio and shields the origin from many edge requests. Origin Access Control is how you lock an S3 origin so only CloudFront can read it.
Global Accelerator does not cache anything. It gives you two static anycast IP addresses; traffic enters the AWS backbone at the nearest edge and travels privately to your endpoints, which cuts jitter and hop count. It works for any TCP or UDP port, not just HTTP, it health-checks endpoints and fails traffic over between Regions in seconds, and the static IPs make it the answer whenever clients must allow-list fixed addresses. Route 53 latency-based routing simply hands out the DNS record for the lowest-latency Region — it is DNS-level, so failover is bounded by TTL and client caching, and it does nothing for the transport path.
concepts.exam_tests: 'Cacheable static or dynamic content, global viewers' is CloudFront. 'Non-HTTP protocol, gaming, VoIP, MQTT, UDP' or 'static IP addresses for firewall allow-listing' or 'fast regional failover measured in seconds' is Global Accelerator. 'Send users to the closest Region' with no other constraint is Route 53 latency routing. When both CloudFront and Global Accelerator appear, ask whether the content is cacheable — if yes, CloudFront.

example.scenario: A multiplayer game server uses UDP and runs in three Regions. Players report inconsistent latency and long recovery times when a Region becomes unhealthy. The game client is hard-coded with a small set of server IP addresses.
example.answer: Put AWS Global Accelerator in front of the regional endpoints and use its two static anycast IPs.
example.why: CloudFront is HTTP and HTTPS only, so it cannot carry UDP game traffic at all. Global Accelerator gives fixed anycast IPs that satisfy the hard-coded client, routes over the AWS backbone to cut jitter, and shifts traffic away from an unhealthy Region within seconds. Route 53 would need a DNS change and is throttled by client-side TTL caching.

rows: Distributed edge IPs, use a CNAME
Static sites, media, APIs with cacheable responses
Gaming, IoT, VoIP, non-HTTP, IP allow-lists
Steering users to the nearest Region

gotchas: CloudFront Functions run only on viewer request and response, are JavaScript-only, cannot make network calls or read the body, and are for header rewrites, redirects and simple auth. Lambda@Edge can call other services, access the request body, and runs at origin request and response too.
Origin Access Control replaced Origin Access Identity and additionally supports Lambda function URLs and SSE-KMS S3 origins.
Global Accelerator has no cache, so it never reduces origin load — only path quality and failover time.
A cache-hit ratio problem is usually a cache-key problem: forwarding all cookies, headers or query strings fragments the cache.
Origin Shield is a paid extra regional cache layer, chosen when many edge locations independently miss to the same origin.
Route 53 alias records are free and can point at the zone apex; CNAMEs cannot be used at the apex.

concepts.name: Hybrid links: Direct Connect vs Site-to-Site VPN vs Client VPN
concepts.explain:
Direct Connect is a private physical circuit from your network into an AWS Direct Connect location. Dedicated connections come at 1, 10, 100 or 400 Gbps; hosted connections from a partner start far lower and are how you get sub-1 Gbps. Because it is a dedicated circuit, it delivers consistent bandwidth and predictable latency that the public internet cannot promise — and it takes weeks or months to provision, which is why 'we need it now' answers pair a Site-to-Site VPN as the interim link. Crucially, Direct Connect is not encrypted by default: if the stem requires encryption in transit you either run an IPsec VPN over a public virtual interface, enable MACsec on supported dedicated ports, or accept the private-circuit argument only when encryption is not required.
Virtual interfaces define what the circuit reaches. A private VIF reaches VPC resources through a virtual private gateway or Direct Connect gateway. A public VIF reaches AWS public endpoints such as S3 and DynamoDB over public IPs, still on the private circuit. A transit VIF connects to Transit Gateway through a Direct Connect gateway, which is how one circuit serves many VPCs across Regions. Link Aggregation Groups bond up to four connections for more bandwidth and link redundancy.
Site-to-Site VPN is IPsec over the internet with two tunnels per connection, each capped at about 1.25 Gbps. To exceed that you terminate multiple VPN connections on a Transit Gateway and use ECMP to spread traffic across them. Client VPN is the unrelated remote-user product: individual laptops connecting into the VPC.
concepts.exam_tests: 'Consistent, predictable bandwidth and latency for a hybrid workload' is Direct Connect. 'Needs connectivity within days' or 'lowest cost hybrid link' is Site-to-Site VPN. 'Direct Connect but the data must be encrypted' means VPN over Direct Connect or MACsec. 'Needs more than 1.25 Gbps over VPN' means multiple tunnels with ECMP on a Transit Gateway. 'Highly available Direct Connect' means two connections at two different Direct Connect locations, and a VPN backup is the cheaper resilient option.

example.scenario: A company has a 10 Gbps Direct Connect link to AWS. A compliance requirement states that all data traversing any network outside the company data centre must be encrypted in transit. Network engineers claim Direct Connect already satisfies this.
example.answer: Run an IPsec Site-to-Site VPN over the Direct Connect public virtual interface (or enable MACsec on the dedicated connection).
example.why: Direct Connect is private but unencrypted at layer 2 and 3, so a compliance requirement for encryption in transit is not met by the circuit alone. Layering IPsec on top gives encryption while keeping the dedicated path's predictable performance. Moving entirely to an internet VPN would satisfy encryption but throw away the bandwidth and latency consistency the company paid for.

rows: ~1.25 Gbps per tunnel; scale with ECMP over TGW
Not encrypted by default (add IPsec or MACsec)
Port hours plus lower data-transfer-out rates
Low hourly plus standard data transfer
Two connections at two DX locations, or DX plus VPN backup
Two tunnels per connection, two customer gateways

gotchas: A single Direct Connect connection is a single point of failure; high availability needs a second connection, ideally at a different Direct Connect location.
Private VIF reaches VPC private IPs; public VIF reaches AWS public service endpoints. Choosing the wrong VIF type is a common trap.
A Direct Connect gateway is what lets one connection serve VPCs in multiple Regions; a virtual private gateway alone is tied to one VPC.
MACsec is available only on dedicated 10, 100 and 400 Gbps connections at supported locations.
Accelerated Site-to-Site VPN routes the tunnel over Global Accelerator to improve internet path quality — the answer for 'VPN performance is inconsistent across long distances'.
Client VPN is for individual users; it never answers a data-centre-to-VPC question.
numbers: Site-to-Site VPN: 2 tunnels per connection, ~1.25 Gbps per tunnel
Direct Connect dedicated: 1, 10, 100, 400 Gbps; LAG bonds up to 4 connections

concepts.name: Connecting many VPCs: peering, Transit Gateway, PrivateLink, and MTU
concepts.explain:
VPC peering is a one-to-one, non-transitive link. Two peered VPCs route to each other directly with no bandwidth bottleneck and no extra hop, but a VPC cannot route through a peer to reach a third VPC, and the CIDR blocks must not overlap. With more than a handful of VPCs the number of peering connections grows quadratically, which is the classic setup for the Transit Gateway answer. Transit Gateway is a regional hub that attaches VPCs, VPN connections and Direct Connect transit VIFs, routes transitively between them, supports route tables for segmentation, peers with Transit Gateways in other Regions over encrypted AWS backbone links, and is the only one of these that supports multicast.
PrivateLink solves a different problem: exposing one service, not connecting whole networks. The provider puts a Network Load Balancer (or Gateway Load Balancer) behind an endpoint service; consumers create interface endpoints in their own VPCs. Traffic is one-way — consumers reach the service, the service cannot reach back into consumer VPCs — overlapping CIDRs are irrelevant because nothing is routed, and it scales to thousands of consumers without touching route tables.
MTU is the quiet performance detail. Inside a VPC and over a Direct Connect private virtual interface you get 9001-byte jumbo frames. Traffic across a Transit Gateway or a Direct Connect transit VIF is capped at 8500 bytes. Anything crossing an internet gateway, a Site-to-Site VPN or an inter-Region peering connection falls back to 1500 bytes, which is why 'throughput dropped after we moved traffic onto the VPN' has a physical explanation.
concepts.exam_tests: 'Dozens or hundreds of VPCs, simplify routing' is Transit Gateway. 'Two VPCs only, lowest cost, lowest latency' is peering. 'Expose a SaaS or internal service to other accounts, including ones with overlapping CIDRs, without exposing the whole network' is PrivateLink. 'Multicast' is Transit Gateway. 'Transitive routing' is Transit Gateway — peering never routes transitively. Watch for overlapping CIDR blocks, which instantly eliminate peering and Transit Gateway attachments and leave PrivateLink.

example.scenario: A software company hosts an internal API in its own VPC and needs to make it available to 200 customer VPCs across many AWS accounts. Several customers use the same private CIDR range as the provider, and customers must not be able to reach anything else in the provider's VPC.
example.answer: Publish the API through an AWS PrivateLink endpoint service backed by a Network Load Balancer, and have each customer create an interface endpoint.
example.why: PrivateLink exposes a single service rather than a network, so overlapping CIDRs are irrelevant and connectivity is one-way from consumer to provider. VPC peering fails outright on overlapping CIDRs and would need 200 connections. Transit Gateway would connect the networks rather than one endpoint, which breaks the isolation requirement.

rows: Two or a few VPCs, full network access, no extra hop
Many VPCs, VPNs and DX in one routing domain; multicast
Expose one service to many accounts with isolation
Encrypted hybrid link over the internet, fast to set up

gotchas: VPC peering is not transitive and does not support edge-to-edge routing through a NAT gateway, VPN or Direct Connect in the peer VPC.
Transit Gateway adds a small per-attachment hourly charge and per-GB processing, so for exactly two VPCs peering is cheaper and lower latency.
Interface endpoints (PrivateLink) cost per hour and per GB; gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB are free — that cost contrast is tested constantly.
Transit Gateway inter-Region peering encrypts traffic over the AWS backbone and does not support multicast or security-group referencing across the peering.
MTU falls to 1500 over VPN, internet gateway and inter-Region peering; jumbo frames are 9001 in-VPC and 8500 through a Transit Gateway.
PrivateLink requires an NLB (or GWLB) in the provider VPC — an option using an ALB as the endpoint-service target is wrong unless it is fronted by an NLB.
numbers: MTU: 9001 in-VPC and DX private VIF, 8500 via Transit Gateway, 1500 over VPN, IGW and inter-Region peering

sections.title: Data ingestion and analytics
sections.summary: Streaming choice hinges on whether you need replay and custom processing or just delivery; analytics choice hinges on whether the data stays in S3 and how often you query it.

concepts.name: Streaming ingestion: Kinesis Data Streams vs Firehose vs Managed Flink vs MSK
concepts.explain:
Kinesis Data Streams is a durable, replayable log. Capacity is measured in shards: each shard takes 1 MB per second or 1,000 records per second of writes and serves 2 MB per second of reads shared across all standard consumers. Enhanced fan-out gives each registered consumer its own dedicated 2 MB per second per shard with roughly 70-millisecond latency, which is the answer when multiple applications read the same stream and interfere with one another. Data is retained from 24 hours up to 365 days, so consumers can replay. On-demand mode removes shard management and scales automatically.
Firehose (renamed Amazon Data Firehose) is not a stream — it is a delivery pipeline. You cannot replay from it and there are no shards or consumers; it buffers by size or time (roughly 1 to 128 MB, or 0 to 900 seconds — zero buffering is supported for the lowest delivery lag) and writes to S3, Redshift, OpenSearch, Splunk or an HTTP endpoint, optionally transforming records with Lambda and converting JSON to Parquet or ORC on the way. That buffering is why Firehose is near-real-time, not real-time.
Managed Service for Apache Flink is the stateful processing layer on top: windowed aggregations, joins across streams, anomaly detection in SQL or Java. MSK is managed Apache Kafka, and it wins exactly when the stem mentions Kafka APIs, existing Kafka producers and consumers, or a migration from a self-managed Kafka cluster.
concepts.exam_tests: 'Multiple consumers, replay, ordered per key, real-time' is Kinesis Data Streams. 'Simply load streaming data into S3, Redshift or OpenSearch with the least operational overhead' is Firehose. 'ProvisionedThroughputExceeded errors' means add shards or fix the partition key. 'Existing Kafka application' is MSK. 'Compute a rolling five-minute average over the stream' is Managed Service for Apache Flink. If the stem says 'no code to manage and near-real-time is fine', Firehose beats Streams.

example.scenario: A telemetry pipeline ingests 8 MB per second into a Kinesis data stream configured with 6 shards. A newly added analytics consumer causes the existing alerting consumer to fall behind and see read throttling. The team wants both consumers to read at full speed.
example.answer: Increase the shard count to cover the ingest rate and register both consumers for enhanced fan-out.
example.why: Six shards give only 6 MB per second of write capacity against an 8 MB per second ingest, so the stream is under-provisioned, and standard consumers share a single 2 MB per second per shard read budget, which is why the second consumer starved the first. Enhanced fan-out gives each consumer its own dedicated read throughput per shard. Switching to Firehose would lose the replay and multi-consumer capability entirely.

rows: Multiple consumers, ordering, replay, custom processing
Just deliver to S3, Redshift, OpenSearch or Splunk
Kafka API compatibility or migrating existing Kafka

gotchas: Firehose cannot replay and has no consumers — any requirement for reprocessing historical records eliminates it.
Ordering in Kinesis is guaranteed only within a shard, and the partition key decides the shard, so a poor partition key both breaks ordering assumptions and creates hot shards.
Firehose to Redshift actually stages through S3 and issues COPY; there is no direct streaming write.
Format conversion to Parquet in Firehose needs a Glue Data Catalog table to supply the schema.
Kinesis on-demand mode removes shard management but costs more per GB at steady high volume than a well-sized provisioned stream.

SQS is not a streaming service: no replay after deletion, no multiple independent consumers of the same message, no ordering except FIFO. If the stem needs several consumers to see every record, it is Kinesis or SNS fan-out, not SQS.
numbers: Per shard: 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s in, 2 MB/s out shared
Enhanced fan-out: 2 MB/s per consumer per shard, ~70 ms
Retention 24 hours default, up to 365 days
Firehose buffer: 1–128 MB or 0–900 seconds (zero buffering supported)

concepts.name: Analytics engines: Athena, Glue, EMR and Redshift Spectrum
concepts.explain:
Athena is serverless SQL over data sitting in S3. You pay per terabyte scanned — roughly five dollars — so every Athena performance and cost question has the same three-part answer: partition the data, convert it to a columnar format such as Parquet or ORC, and compress it. Partitioning lets Athena skip whole directories; columnar formats let it read only the columns in the SELECT; compression shrinks what remains. Together they routinely cut scanned bytes by an order of magnitude.
Glue is the serverless ETL and metadata layer. The Glue Data Catalog is the shared Hive-compatible metastore that Athena, EMR, Redshift Spectrum and Lake Formation all read. Crawlers infer schema and partitions from S3 automatically. Glue jobs run Spark without a cluster, and DataBrew provides visual, no-code preparation for analysts.
EMR is managed Hadoop, Spark, Hive, Presto and HBase on clusters you shape. It wins when you need specific framework versions, custom libraries, long-running Spark jobs, or fine-grained cost control — notably running task nodes on Spot while keeping core nodes On-Demand, because core nodes hold HDFS data. EMR Serverless removes cluster sizing. Redshift Spectrum is the fourth option and is only relevant when a Redshift cluster already exists and you want to join warehouse tables to S3 data.
concepts.exam_tests: 'Occasional ad-hoc SQL over S3 with no infrastructure' is Athena. 'Reduce Athena cost or query time' is partition plus Parquet plus compress. 'Discover schema automatically' is a Glue crawler. 'Serverless ETL with no cluster' is Glue jobs; 'visual data preparation for non-engineers' is DataBrew. 'Existing Spark or Hadoop jobs, custom frameworks, or cost control with Spot' is EMR. 'Join S3 data to tables inside an existing Redshift cluster' is Spectrum.

example.scenario: Analysts query a 60 TB S3 dataset of JSON logs with Athena. Queries almost always filter on a single day and select four of the forty available columns, but each query scans the full dataset and the monthly Athena bill is high.
example.answer: Convert the data to partitioned, compressed Parquet (partitioned by date) and repoint the Glue table at it.
example.why: Athena charges by bytes scanned, and JSON is row-oriented, so every query reads all forty columns for all days. Partitioning by date lets Athena prune to one partition, and Parquet lets it read only the four requested columns; together that cuts scanned bytes dramatically. Moving to Redshift would work technically but adds a cluster and a load pipeline the stem does not ask for.

rows: Ad-hoc SQL, no infrastructure, data stays in S3
Serverless Spark ETL + Data Catalog + crawlers
Schema discovery, scheduled ETL, no cluster to run
Existing big-data frameworks, custom libraries, heavy sustained jobs
Per TB scanned, plus the cluster
Joining S3 data with tables already in Redshift
Repeated complex analytical SQL with high concurrency

gotchas: Athena cost is driven by bytes scanned, not by rows returned — LIMIT does not reduce the bill.
EMR core nodes hold HDFS data, so putting them on Spot risks data loss; only task nodes belong on Spot.
Glue crawlers cost money per run and are unnecessary when the schema is stable and defined manually.
Redshift Spectrum requires a Redshift cluster or serverless workgroup; if there is no warehouse in the scenario, Athena is the cheaper answer.
Lake Formation adds column-, row- and cell-level permissions on top of the Glue Catalog and is the answer for 'restrict analysts to a subset of columns across Athena, Redshift and EMR'.
OpenSearch UltraWarm stores indexes in S3 for read-only, much cheaper long-tail log retention; cold storage is cheaper still but must be attached before querying.
numbers: Athena: about $5 per TB scanned
Parquet plus partitioning routinely cuts scanned bytes by 90 percent or more
concepts.mnemonic: Athena question? Partition, Parquet, comPress — the three P's.

concepts.name: Governance and consumption: Lake Formation, QuickSight, OpenSearch tiers
concepts.explain:
Once data lands in S3, three services complete the picture. Lake Formation sits over the Glue Data Catalog and centralises fine-grained permissions — database, table, column, row and even cell level — which are then enforced consistently whether the analyst queries through Athena, Redshift Spectrum, EMR or Glue. It is the answer whenever the requirement is 'different teams see different columns of the same table' with the least operational overhead, because the alternative is hand-crafting S3 bucket policies per team.
QuickSight is the BI layer: dashboards, embedded analytics, and SPICE, an in-memory engine that caches a dataset so dashboards render without re-querying the source. That caching is the standard answer to 'dashboards are slow and hammering Redshift'.
OpenSearch Service handles search and log analytics, and its tiered storage is a favourite of cost-and-performance questions. Hot storage lives on the data nodes' EBS or local NVMe for fast writes and queries. UltraWarm keeps indexes in S3 with local caching for read-only access at a fraction of the cost. Cold storage is the cheapest tier, also in S3, but an index must be attached back into UltraWarm before it can be queried. Index State Management policies move indexes down the tiers automatically by age.
concepts.exam_tests: 'Column-level or row-level access control across the data lake with the least effort' is Lake Formation. 'Dashboards for business users, embedded in an application' is QuickSight; 'dashboards are slow' points at SPICE. 'Keep 18 months of logs searchable but cut cost' is OpenSearch UltraWarm and cold with an ISM policy. 'Natural-language questions about the data' is QuickSight Q.

example.scenario: A company keeps 18 months of application logs in OpenSearch Service. Only the last 14 days are queried regularly; older data is searched a few times a month during investigations. Storage cost has become the largest line item.
example.answer: Keep 14 days in hot storage and use an Index State Management policy to move older indexes to UltraWarm, then to cold storage.
example.why: UltraWarm backs indexes with S3 while keeping them directly searchable, cutting storage cost sharply for read-only data, and cold storage cuts it further for the rarely touched tail. Moving everything to S3 as raw files would satisfy cost but lose the search interface the investigations need. Adding data nodes addresses capacity but increases the cost the stem is trying to reduce.

rows: Roughly an order of magnitude cheaper
Must be attached to UltraWarm before querying

gotchas: UltraWarm indexes are read-only — you cannot write new documents into them.
Cold storage indexes cannot be queried until reattached, so they fail any 'immediately searchable' requirement.
Lake Formation permissions only apply to consumers that go through the catalog; direct S3 access with a permissive bucket policy bypasses them.
QuickSight SPICE data is a snapshot and needs a refresh schedule — dashboards will show stale data otherwise.
QuickSight Enterprise edition is required for row-level security, VPC connectivity and Active Directory integration.
OpenSearch Serverless removes node sizing but is billed in OpenSearch Compute Units and is not always cheaper for steady heavy workloads.

sections.title: Getting data into AWS
sections.summary: Compute the transfer time first: if the wire cannot finish in about a week, ship a Snow device; otherwise the protocol the source speaks picks the service.

concepts.name: Online transfer vs Snow: DataSync, Transfer Family, and the one-week rule
concepts.explain:
Start every migration question with arithmetic. A 1 Gbps link moves roughly 10.8 TB per day at theoretical line rate, and realistically closer to 8 TB per day once you allow for overhead and shared use. Divide the dataset by that and if the answer exceeds about a week, the exam wants a Snow device. A Snowcone holds 8 TB on HDD or 14 TB on SSD and is small enough to ship anywhere; a Snowball Edge Storage Optimized device holds about 80 TB usable, with newer devices reaching around 210 TB, and multiple devices run in parallel for petabyte-scale moves.
When the wire is adequate, the protocol decides. DataSync is the bulk online transfer engine: an agent on-premises reads NFS, SMB, HDFS or self-managed object storage and writes into S3, EFS or any FSx flavour, with scheduling, bandwidth throttling, incremental transfer, in-flight validation and metadata preservation. It also moves data between AWS storage services. Transfer Family is a different job entirely: it provides managed SFTP, FTPS, FTP and AS2 endpoints so external partners keep using the protocol they already have while the bytes land in S3 or EFS. If the stem mentions partners, existing SFTP scripts or an FTP server to retire, it is Transfer Family; if it mentions a one-off or recurring bulk copy of a filesystem, it is DataSync.
concepts.exam_tests: Do the maths whenever a dataset size and a link speed both appear — that pairing is the signal. 'Partners upload over SFTP and cannot change their process' is Transfer Family. 'Migrate 200 TB of NFS shares to EFS on a schedule with bandwidth limits' is DataSync. 'No connectivity, remote site, edge processing' is Snowcone or Snowball Edge. 'Ongoing incremental sync after the initial bulk move' is DataSync following a Snow transfer.

example.scenario: A media company must move 300 TB of archived footage from an on-premises NAS to Amazon S3. The site has a 500 Mbps internet link that is also used by the business, and the migration must complete within one month.
example.answer: Order multiple AWS Snowball Edge devices and ship the data, then use DataSync for the incremental delta.
example.why: At 500 Mbps, even at full line rate, 300 TB takes roughly 55 days, and the link is shared, so the transfer cannot meet a one-month deadline over the wire. Snowball Edge devices move the bulk offline in days. DataSync alone would be correct only if the link had the headroom, and Transfer Acceleration improves upload paths but cannot create bandwidth that does not exist.

rows: Online bulk copy, scheduled or one-off
NFS, SMB, HDFS, self-managed object, AWS-to-AWS
Bulk migration or recurring sync over an adequate link
External partners must keep their existing protocol
NFS or S3 API on the device
Link too slow or absent; transfer would take over a week
On-premises systems keep running and need cloud-backed storage
Moving a live database with change data capture

gotchas: 1 Gbps is about 10.8 TB per day at theory and roughly 8 TB per day in practice — memorise this to do the arithmetic fast.
Snowball Edge Compute Optimized exists for edge processing (and GPU workloads) at a disconnected site, not just for shipping bytes.
AWS Snowmobile has been discontinued; do not pick it for exabyte-scale scenarios in current material.
DataSync needs an agent for on-premises sources but not for AWS-to-AWS transfers.
Transfer Family charges per endpoint hour whether used or not, plus per GB — so it loses on cost for a one-off bulk move.
S3 Transfer Acceleration helps long-distance uploads over a healthy link; it does nothing when the bottleneck is raw local bandwidth.
numbers: Snowcone 8 TB HDD / 14 TB SSD; Snowball Edge Storage Optimized ~80 TB usable (newer devices ~210 TB)
1 Gbps ≈ 10.8 TB/day at line rate; assume ~8 TB/day realistically
DataSync: up to about 10 Gbps per agent — add agents (or Snow) beyond that
Rule of thumb: more than about one week over the wire means use Snow

concepts.name: Storage Gateway: File, Volume cached vs stored, and Tape
concepts.explain:
Storage Gateway is for hybrid situations where on-premises systems must keep working unchanged while their data is backed by AWS. It comes in four shapes and the exam tests the distinction between two of them relentlessly. S3 File Gateway presents an NFS or SMB share; files written to it become S3 objects one-for-one, with a local cache for recently accessed data, so on-premises applications get a file interface over S3 and lifecycle policies apply to the objects. FSx File Gateway does the same for FSx for Windows, giving remote offices a low-latency local cache of an SMB share.
Volume Gateway presents iSCSI block volumes. In cached mode the primary copy of the data lives in S3 and only the hot subset is cached locally, so you get effectively unlimited capacity with a small local footprint. In stored mode the primary copy stays on-premises for full low-latency local access and is asynchronously backed up to S3 as EBS snapshots. The discriminator is one sentence: cached means primary in AWS, stored means primary on-premises. Tape Gateway presents a virtual tape library over iSCSI so existing backup software (NetBackup, Veeam, Commvault) writes tapes that actually land in S3 and Glacier, which is the answer to any 'eliminate physical tape' question.
concepts.exam_tests: 'Existing backup software writing to tape, want to stop buying tapes' is Tape Gateway. 'On-premises applications need low-latency access to all local data with cloud backup' is Volume Gateway stored. 'Local storage capacity is exhausted, keep only hot data on-site' is Volume Gateway cached. 'On-premises servers need an NFS or SMB share whose contents are S3 objects' is S3 File Gateway. If the scenario has no on-premises component, Storage Gateway is a distractor.

example.scenario: A manufacturing plant's application writes to an on-premises iSCSI volume and requires low-latency access to the entire 20 TB dataset. The company wants offsite backups in AWS without changing the application or accepting higher read latency.
example.answer: Deploy a Volume Gateway in stored mode so the full dataset stays local and is asynchronously snapshotted to S3.
example.why: Stored mode keeps the primary copy on-premises, which is the only way to guarantee low-latency access to the entire dataset, while EBS snapshots go to AWS for offsite protection. Cached mode would put the primary copy in S3 and serve only hot blocks locally, adding latency for cold reads. S3 File Gateway presents a file interface, not the iSCSI block device the application expects.

rows: File share whose contents are usable S3 objects
Branch office needs low-latency access to a Windows share
Local capacity is the constraint; keep only hot blocks on-site
Full dataset must stay local; back up offsite
Replace physical tape libraries, keep backup software

gotchas: Cached versus stored is the most-tested pair here: cached puts the primary copy in AWS, stored keeps it on-premises.
S3 File Gateway writes real S3 objects, so lifecycle policies, replication and other S3 features apply — that is why it beats a plain sync script.
Tape Gateway integrates with existing backup applications over the standard VTL interface, so no backup software change is needed.
Storage Gateway runs as a VM or a hardware appliance on-premises (or on EC2 for testing) and needs a local disk for cache and upload buffer.
A Storage Gateway answer in a scenario with no on-premises footprint is always wrong.
For a one-time migration DataSync is cheaper and faster than File Gateway; File Gateway is for ongoing hybrid access.
concepts.mnemonic: Cached = Cloud holds it. Stored = Site holds it.

concepts.name: Event-driven ingestion: S3 notifications, EventBridge and AppFlow
concepts.explain:
Once objects land in S3, processing should start by itself. S3 Event Notifications fire on object creation, deletion, restore and replication events, and can target SNS, SQS or Lambda directly — the simple, low-latency path when one bucket triggers one or two consumers. Sending S3 events to EventBridge instead unlocks richer content-based filtering, more than twenty targets, archive and replay of events, and cross-account routing, which is why 'multiple downstream systems' or 'need to replay events' points at EventBridge. The general design rule is a fan-out pattern: S3 to SNS, SNS to several SQS queues, each queue feeding its own consumer, so a slow consumer never blocks the others.
AppFlow is the different door into AWS: a managed connector service that pulls data from SaaS applications such as Salesforce, SAP, Slack, Zendesk and Google Analytics into S3, Redshift or Snowflake on a schedule or on an event, with field mapping, filtering and validation, and no code. When a scenario says 'ingest data from a third-party SaaS product with the least development effort', AppFlow is the answer and building a Lambda that calls the vendor API is the trap.
concepts.exam_tests: 'Process each uploaded file automatically' is an S3 event notification to Lambda. 'Several independent systems must each react to the same upload' is S3 to SNS fan-out or S3 to EventBridge. 'Need to replay past events or filter on object metadata' is EventBridge. 'Pull records from Salesforce into S3 without writing code' is AppFlow. Anything describing a polling loop or a scheduled scan of a bucket is a distractor when an event-driven option exists.

example.scenario: Every image uploaded to an S3 bucket must be resized, virus-scanned and catalogued by three independent teams' services. Today a single Lambda function does all three and a failure in one step blocks the others.
example.answer: Publish the S3 event to an SNS topic and subscribe three SQS queues, one per consuming service.
example.why: SNS fan-out delivers a copy of each event to every subscriber, and the intervening SQS queues decouple the consumers so one failing or slow service cannot block the rest, with retries and a dead-letter queue per consumer. Adding more Lambda concurrency to the monolithic function does not remove the coupling. S3 can also publish to EventBridge for the same fan-out with richer filtering, which is equally defensible when advanced routing is required.

rows: Simple, direct, one or two consumers
Many consumers, complex routing, audit and replay
Many queues, each with its own consumer
Independent consumers that must not block each other

gotchas: S3 event notification filtering supports only prefix and suffix; anything richer requires EventBridge.
Only EventBridge offers event archive and replay — S3 notifications and plain SNS do not.
Putting SQS between the event source and the consumer is the standard answer for buffering bursts and protecting a downstream system, and it gives you retries plus a dead-letter queue.
Direct S3-to-Lambda invocation has no queue, so a Lambda throttle can drop work; the durable pattern goes through SQS.
AppFlow supports both scheduled and event-triggered flows, and it beats a hand-written Lambda integration on 'least development effort'.
EventBridge Scheduler replaces CloudWatch Events rules for cron-style triggers at scale and supports one-time schedules.
